sentences.text: The captioned writ petition is filed seeking mandamus against the respondents to initiate acquisition proceedings and pay compensation to the petitioners for having utilized the petitioners land for the purpose of formation of canal.
2. Petitioners' grievance is that respondents have utilized the petition land bearing R.S.No.71/3+4 in 2005- 06 for the purpose of formation of canal.
To substantiate that their land is utilized without acquiring the land, petitioners have placed reliance on the endorsement issued by respondent No.3 vide Annexure-K.
Reliance is also placed on Annexure-G which is spot inspection done by respondent No.3.

Placing reliance on these two documents, petitioners are before this court alleging inaction on the part of the respondents in not considering the representation dated 28.09.2021 vide Annexure-F.
3.

Heard the learned counsel for the petitioners, learned standing counsel for respondent Nos.2 to 4,
NC: 2023:KHC-D:10854 learned HCGP for respondent Nos.1 and 5 and perused the material on record.
4. On perusal of Annexures-K and G, it is clearly evident that respondent Nos.2 to 4 have utilized the petitioners land for formation of canal.
5. Soon after the fundamental right to property was abolished, the supreme court recognized the value of the right to property as a fundamental right in Bhim Singh v. Union of India (1981).

entities.text: Bhim Singh v. Union of India (1981)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the absence of this fundamental right to property, it relied on the second Fundamental Right of Property, inamely the idea of reasonableness under article 14, to invalidate certain provisions of the urban land ceiling legislation.

Though the right to property is not a fundamental right, it is a valuable constitutional right, according to the Supreme Court in the case of B. K. Ravichandra v.
Union of India(2020), which ordered the Centre to return the land to its owners.

entities.text:
B. K. Ravichandra v.
Union of India(2020)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Supreme Court's decisions and the history of the right to property reveal that, while its primacy as a fundamental NC: 2023:KHC-D:10854 right has been questioned, it is nonetheless protected by the rule of law.
This court's expanding jurisprudence also demonstrates that it is a valuable right that guarantees basic liberties and economic liberty.
Article 300-A's wording is crucial, and its resemblance to Articles 21 and 265 cannot be overlooked-they are, after all, a guarantee of the supremacy of the rule of law.

In a more recent case of Bajranga v. State of Madhya Pradesh(2021),

3 "right to property is still a constitutional right under article 300A of the Constitution," the Supreme Court has ruled in a case where the government took ownership of surplus land even though there was none.

entities.text: Bajranga v. State of Madhya Pradesh(2021)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The deprivation of a right can only be done in conformity with the legal procedure."
The Courts have also acknowledged the State's interference in the citizen's right to property.

It was held in Ravindran v. The District Collector, Vellore District (2020) that the government has no authority to interfere with a citizen's right to property unless it is done in compliance with the law which was later on reiterated in NC: 2023:KHC-D:10854 Jayalakshmi and Ors. v. State of Tamil Nadu(2021).

entities.text: Ravindran v. The District Collector, Vellore District (2020)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: 2023:KHC-D:10854 Jayalakshmi and Ors. v. State of Tamil Nadu(2021)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Recently, the Madras High Court made a noteworthy statement, saying that under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution, the Right to Property has a tight relationship with the Right to Life.

The Apex Court in Vidya Devi Vs. The State of Himachala Pradesh and others observed that the State cannot dispossess a citizen of his property except in accordance with the procedure established by law.

entities.text: Vidya Devi Vs. The State of Himachala Pradesh and others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The obligation to pay compensation, though not expressly included in Article 300 A, can be inferred in that Article.

To forcibly dispossess a person of his private property, without following due process of law, would be violative of a human right, as also the constitutional right under Article 300 A of the Constitution.'
6.
In the light of the discussion made supra, I am of the view that if petitioners land is utilized by the respondents, the petitioners are legally entitled to claim compensation.
Equally, respondents are bound to initiate NC: 2023:KHC-D:10854 acquisition proceedings and pay compensation.
Since there is inaction on the part of the respondents in not acquiring the petitioners land, I am of the view that this is a fit case to issue mandamus to the respondents.

Accordingly, I pass the following:
ORDER i) The writ petition is allowed.
ii) Respondents are hereby directed to consider the representation dated 28.09.2021 and take appropriate action by taking cognizance of Annexures-G and K and initiate acquisition proceedings under the 2013 Act and pay compensation to the petitioners,
in accordance with law.
iii) This exercise shall be completed within a period of six months from the date of receipt of copy of this order Sd/-
